ubo_and_aml_profiling.statutory_law_governance: The principal statutory framework is the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 (AML/CFT Act), the Companies Act 1993, the Companies (Beneficial Ownership Register) Amendment Act 2023, and regulations made under the Financial Markets Authority (AML/CFT) Rules. Beneficial ownership information for New Zealand companies is filed with the Registrar of Companies and the restricted beneficial ownership register is accessible only to government agencies and law enforcement, not to the public.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certificate of Incorporation (certified copy issued by the New Zealand Companies Office)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: New Zealand Companies Office (Registrar of Companies)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: For use in an Apostille Convention State: obtain the certified copy from the Companies Office and apply to the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs for an Apostille. For use in a non-Apostille State: obtain the certified copy, have it authenticated by the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs, and then obtain consular legalization from the destination country's embassy or consulate in New Zealand. Never combine Apostille and consular legalization in the same chain.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certificate of Good Standing (Certificate of Compliance / certificate of no objection)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: New Zealand Companies Office (Registrar of Companies)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague path: issue the certificate, then apostille it through the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs for use in a member state. Non-Hague path: authenticate the certificate through the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs and then complete consular legalization at the receiving state's mission in New Zealand. Use only one authentication path.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Board Resolution appointing a representative and Power of Attorney
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Board of directors of the New Zealand limited company, notarized by a New Zealand notary public
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: If the receiving state is a Hague member, notarize the directors' signatures and then obtain an Apostille from the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs. If the receiving state is not a Hague member, notarize the instrument, have it authenticated by the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs, and then legalize it at the receiving state's consulate in New Zealand. The two paths are separate and must not be chained.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Articles of Association (constitution of the company)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: New Zealand limited company (adopted by subscriber directors), certified as a true copy by the company secretary
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: For Hague member destinations: certify the constitutional document, then apostille it via the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs. For non-Hague destinations: certify the document, authenticate it through the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs, then obtain consular legalization from the destination country's consular post in New Zealand. No sequence may use both mechanisms.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Bank Reference Letter (bank-to-bank or bank-to-customer due diligence confirmation)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: The New Zealand trading bank maintaining the proposed corporate account (e.g., ANZ Bank New Zealand, ASB Bank, Bank of New Zealand, or Westpac New Zealand)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: The bank's authorized signatory must sign the letter before a notary public. For Hague states, notarization is followed by a New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs Apostille. For non-Hague states, notarization is followed by Department of Internal Affairs authentication and then consular legalization by the receiving state's embassy or consulate in New Zealand. Do not add Apostille after consular legalization.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Consent to Act as Director and Director Identification Form
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: The appointed director (New Zealand-resident and overseas director) and the New Zealand Companies Office
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: For Hague member states, notarize the director's signature on the Consent to Act form and apostille it through the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs. For non-member states, notarize the signature, authenticate through the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs, then legalize at the receiving country's consulate in New Zealand. Use exclusively one path per document.

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: The company must screen all shareholders, directors, UBOs, authorized signatories, and beneficial owners in real time against the United Nations Security Council Consolidated Sanctions List, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) SDN and sanctions lists, the New Zealand Sanctions Act 2022 consolidated list, the New Zealand Police Financial Intelligence Unit list, the Department of Internal Affairs warnings, global PEP databases, HM Treasury sanctions lists, and Interpol Red Notices. Enhanced due diligence is mandatory for any person identified as a politically exposed person (PEP), with written source of wealth and source of funds verification, senior management approval, and 12-monthly reviews. Ongoing monitoring must include adverse media screening and transaction pattern analysis in English and any source language used by the counterparty. The screening results must be retained for at least five years under the AML/CFT Act 2009 record-keeping requirements.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: New Zealand Companies Office company name registration and reservation portal (Companies Register) at companies-register.companiesoffice.govt.nz
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Company names may be in English or te reo Maori, and any non-Latin script must be transliterated into Latin characters using a recognized orthographic romanization standard. The Companies Registrar applies a four-tier naming convention: (1) a name must not be identical to any existing or reserved company name; (2) a name must not be so similar to an existing name that it is likely to mislead or deceive; (3) a name must not contain restricted tokens absent prior written approval from the responsible regulator; and (4) a name must not be prohibited, offensive, imply Crown patronage, or suggest an unlawful purpose. All suffixes and abbreviations are normalized when comparing equivalence.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: If the Registrar refuses a name, the applicant may submit a written application for review under section 23 of the Companies Act 1993 to the Registrar of Companies within 20 working days of the refusal. The review request must set out the proposed company name, the refusal reference, the ground of rejection, and a reasoned submission demonstrating distinctiveness and non-offensiveness, preferably accompanied by a statutory declaration and evidence of prior brand use. The Registrar will issue a written decision, and if the refusal is upheld, the applicant may apply to the High Court of New Zealand for judicial review under the Judicature Amendment Act 1972. A name reservation may be extended before expiry by logging into the Companies Office portal and filing an extension request for an additional 20 working days, subject to the same name availability search.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: The Companies Act 1993 requires every New Zealand company to maintain a registered office in New Zealand at a physical street address where documents can be served and where the office is open to the public during ordinary business hours. A licensed virtual office or commercial postal mailbox at a physical New Zealand street address can satisfy the literal registered-office requirement and will not be rejected by the Companies Office for a low-risk online retail company. However, the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) and New Zealand trading banks will reject an arrangement that lacks a physical operating premise for GST registration, corporate bank account opening, merchant acquiring with Stripe, or Affirm BNPL onboarding because the economic substance test requires a place of business, management premise, bank account records, and inventory or fulfillment arrangements. For ISIC 4791 e-commerce retail, IRD is likely to treat a non-resident-managed company with only a mailbox as a tax shell, re-characterize the permanent establishment risk, or deny GST registration. Therefore the prudent structure is a true serviced office with a managed reception, a New Zealand-resident director and/or office manager, dedicated racking for returns, and local books and records; this materially reduces risk while retaining a virtual administrative front.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Unannounced physical inspection risk matrix: (a) IRD field audits and GST integrity visits are rare for new low-risk online retailers without refund claims, quantified at approximately 5% to 10% in the first year; (b) Companies Office verification officers may send registered mail to the registered office and, if mail is returned, may conduct an unscheduled site confirmation, risk approximately 20% to 30% for a virtual-office address; (c) New Zealand Police and FIU do not physically inspect premises for routine AML/CFT compliance, but a site visit becomes 60% likely if the company is nominated for a suspicious activity report or sanctions watchlist match; (d) banks and payment providers may schedule merchant onboarding verification visits, and a failed site visit will terminate the merchant agreement.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Companies Act 1993 (New Zealand), including sections 12 to 14 (incorporation and constitution), section 19 (company name), section 36 (registered office), section 52 (powers of board), the share issuance and directors duties provisions, and the Companies (Forms and Fees) Regulations 1993
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE), operating through the Companies Register online portal
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Form 6 - Application for Registration of a Company, filed electronically with the New Zealand Companies Register
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: None. The Companies Act 1993 imposes no minimum paid-up capital requirement and no blocked escrow account requirement. At least one share must be subscribed, and the board may allot shares for consideration as resolved, subject to solvency and statutory restrictions.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: THE SOLAR PORTABLE POWER RETAIL NZ LIMITED FIRST BOARD OF DIRECTORS RESOLUTION (Pro-Forma) - Resolution No. 2025-001. WHEREAS: (A) The Company was incorporated under the New Zealand Companies Act 1993 on [date] and holds certificate of incorporation No. [No.] issued by the New Zealand Companies Office. (B) The subscribers listed in the register of members have agreed to subscribe for the ordinary share capital of the Company on the terms set out in the incorporation application. (C) The directors must now approve the formal corporate mechanics required for the Company to commence lawful trading. NOW THEREFORE, IT IS HEREBY RESOLVED AS FOLLOWS: 1. SHARE CAPITAL SUBSCRIPTION AND ALLOTMENT: The board confirms that the initial share subscriptions amounting to 1,000 ordinary shares at NZ$1.00 each, credited as fully paid, have been accepted and the shares are allotted to the subscribers identified in the allocation schedule. The directors are authorized to record the allotment in the register of members, issue certificates for the allotted shares, and file any required notice with the Companies Office. 2. REGISTERED OFFICE: The registered office of the Company shall be at [Legal physical address], New Zealand. The directors are instructed to maintain all statutory records at that office and to comply with the Companies Act concerning notification of the registered office. 3. BANKING: The board authorizes the opening of corporate bank accounts with such bank or banks as selected by management and approves the account signatory mandate. The mandate shall require any two of the directors or the chief executive officer and one director to execute banking instructions and documents. Electronic banking limits are to be established and reviewed semi-annually. 4. STATUTORY OFFICERS: The board appoints [name] as director, [name] as chief executive officer, and [name] as company secretary, an optional statutory office. Each officer is authorized to act within the scope of delegated authority and to hold office until resignation or removal in accordance with the Companies Act 1993. 5. CORPORATE GOVERNANCE: The board acknowledges that all officers owe fiduciary duties of good faith, care, and loyalty to the Company under the Companies Act 1993. Interested-party transactions must be disclosed and approved according to the Act. 6. FILING AUTHORITY: The board delegates to any director or authorised officer the authority to complete and file all statutory returns, pay filing fees, and effectuate this resolution. This resolution is passed by unanimous consent of the board and takes effect immediately.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office - Companies Register online portal (Name Reservation service)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Using the Companies Register online portal, conduct an exact search and a phonetic search for each proposed name. Confirm that the proposed name is not prohibited, reserved, identical, or confusingly similar to an existing company name under the Companies Act 1993. File a formal name reservation application through the prescribed online workflow and obtain the reservation confirmation. Obtain signed consent-to-act-as-director forms from every proposed director, verifying that each director is at least 18 years old, is not disqualified under the Companies Act, and has a valid New Zealand residential address or a New Zealand-resident director appointment where required.
required_dossiers: Proposed company name (up to three variants)
Verified RealMe login account credentials
Full director names, dates of birth, and residential addresses
Signed consent to act as director forms
New Zealand agent for service details if any director is resident overseas
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is refused because it is identical, misleading, or objectionable, submit a fresh reservation application with distinguishing words or request written reasons from the Companies Office. A further correction and resubmission may be filed within the reservation validity period without loss of priority.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Prepare and Submit the Incorporation Application
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office - Companies Register electronic filing window
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Complete Form 6 (Application for Registration of a Company) online. Enter the reserved company name, the physical registered office address in New Zealand, postal address, principal place of business, details of subscribers, proposed share allocations, issue price, and the names and addresses of all first directors. Attach the signed director consent forms and, if desired, the company constitution. Confirm the statutory declarations and beneficial ownership details required by the Companies Register. Pay the prescribed incorporation fee electronically and submit the application for immediate processing by the Registrar.
required_dossiers: Form 6 application completed online
Signed director consent forms
Copy of adopted constitution, if any
Physical New Zealand registered office address
List of shareholders with proposed share allotments
Identification documents for each director or subscriber
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Companies Office issues a requisition or suspends the application, respond in writing with corrected data within the stated statutory deadline, usually 20 working days. Provide notarially certified English translations for any non-English documents and resubmit the affected fields. If the application has been rejected, file a fresh corrected application and pay any applicable refiling fee.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: First Board Meeting, Corporate Governance and Bank Account Opening
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registered office for board papers; commercial bank for account opening; Companies Office for post-incorporation filings
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Convene a properly noticed physical or electronic board meeting, pass the first board resolution approving share allotment, registered office adoption, banking authorization and officer appointments, and execute the minutes. Allot the shares, issue share certificates, and update the register of members. Open a corporate bank account with a tier-1 New Zealand bank, providing the certificate of incorporation, NZBN, director identification, and AML/CFT corporate questionnaire. If officer or address details change during the meeting, file the appropriate Notice of Change of Director or Notice of Change of Registered Office with the Companies Office within the statutory deadline.
required_dossiers: Certificate of incorporation and New Zealand Business Number (NZBN)
Company constitution, if adopted
Signed first board resolution and board minutes
Register of members and share certificates
Director photo identification and proof of residential address
AML/CFT corporate banking questionnaire
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Companies Office queries the change of director or registered office, file the prescribed online notice within the statutory period with corrected supporting documents. If the bank rejects the application under its AML/CFT program, respond to additional information requests, obtain a NZ resident director referral, or escalate within the bank and provide the required beneficial ownership declarations.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Tax, ACC and Regulatory Clearance Registrations
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Inland Revenue Department (IRD); Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC); local territorial authority for premises use
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Register with the Inland Revenue Department for an IRD number, GST registration if expected annual turnover exceeds NZ$60,000 or for voluntary compliance, and PAYE and KiwiSaver obligations if hiring employees. Register with ACC as an employer or self-employed person as applicable. Verify with the local territorial authority that the intended premises are zoned for e-commerce retail use. Confirm that no industrial manufacturing license is required for the direct online retail of portable solar generators and solar panels, and review supplier test certificates and consumer-law compliance under the Fair Trading Act 1986 and Consumer Guarantees Act 1993.
required_dossiers: Certificate of incorporation and NZBN
Director identities and personal tax details
Lease or occupancy agreement for the business premises
Projected revenue and turnover forecast
Supplier product compliance certificates, including battery safety test reports if relevant
ACC employer registration questionnaire, if hiring
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If IRD registration is delayed or rejected, use the IRD escalation service, resubmit corrected details, or engage a licensed tax agent to reconcile the application. If ACC assigns an incorrect levy classification, submit a levy review request with supporting turnover and employee data. For any local council premises query, obtain a certificate of compliance or apply for a discretionary land-use consent under the Resource Management Act 1991.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Not Applicable - New Zealand online direct retail under ISIC 4791 does not require an industrial manufacturing license; premises use is controlled by the local territorial authority only.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Not Applicable - no statutory industrial operating or manufacturing permit is required for pure e-commerce retail sales of portable battery generators and solar panels.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Not Applicable for this retail activity; the New Zealand Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) would be the competent authority only if future manufacturing, discharge, or hazardous waste activities are added.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Not Applicable - no Environmental Impact Assessment, resource consent, or permitted-activity assessment is triggered by ISIC 4791 online retail sales.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Not Applicable - no industrial effluent, VOC, or hazardous waste discharge exists. If warehousing of lithium batteries is later added, storage must be reviewed against the Hazardous Substances (Classes 6-9) Regulations 2001 and Waste Minimisation Act 2008 product stewardship obligations.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Not Applicable for pure online retail. If a commercial service office is occupied, the company must obtain a building warrant of fitness and comply with fire evacuation and fire safety requirements under the Building Act 2004 and Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ) guidelines. No Civil Defence fire permit is required for low-quantity storage of portable power units; large-scale battery storage would require hazardous substances location compliance assessment.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Inland Revenue Department (IRD) of New Zealand; online portal myIR (myir.ird.govt.nz) and the New Zealand Companies Office (for entity registration).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: For a foreign non-resident entity establishing a New Zealand limited company, the procedure is: (1) Incorporate the company with the New Zealand Companies Office via the online portal (NZBN registration); the Companies Office will issue a New Zealand Business Number (NZBN). (2) Apply for an IRD number for the company using the IRD application form IR742 ('Non-resident company tax registration') or through myIR, providing certified copies of the certificate of incorporation, the NZBN confirmation, and proof of directors' identities. (3) If the company expects to make taxable supplies exceeding NZD 60,000 in a 12-month period, or intends to claim input tax credits, it must separately register for GST using form IR356 ('GST registration') or via myIR, supplying the same identification data. (4) The IRD will issue an 8-digit IRD number for income tax purposes and a separate GST registration number (the same IRD number with a GST suffix) upon successful registration. The entire process can be completed remotely; no physical presence or local director is mandated if a registered agent is appointed, though the Companies Office requires a local registered office address.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: None for generic limited companies under New Zealand law. However, if the entity qualifies as a closely held company (five or fewer shareholders), it may elect look-through company (LTC) status under Subpart HB of the Income Tax Act 2007, which allows shareholders to be taxed on their share of the company's income and losses. This election is made via form IR427 and is an annual irrevocable election. No check-the-box or hybrid mismatch elections are available beyond the LTC regime.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: NZD 60,000 of taxable supplies in a 12-month period (including zero-rated supplies) or NZD 60,000 of taxable supplies expected to be made in the next 12 months; voluntary registration is permitted.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: New Zealand does not mandate real-time fiscal clearance or digital stamping. E-invoicing is voluntary and based on the Peppol network. Businesses may issue tax invoices in any format, provided they contain the prescribed GST information under section 24 of the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985, including the supplier's name and GST number, the date of supply, the description, and the total amount payable. For GST purposes, buyers cannot claim input tax credits without a valid tax invoice. There are no API-based clearance requirements for standard B2B/B2C sales.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating applies to the supply of goods exported from New Zealand within 28 days of the time of supply, provided the supplier obtains and holds sufficient evidence of export, including a customs export declaration or a transport document (e.g., bill of lading or airway bill). Additionally, the supply of goods to a non-resident who is not in New Zealand at the time of supply, if the goods are removed from New Zealand by the recipient, is zero-rated under section 11(1)(a) of the GST Act 1985. For services, zero-rating applies to services supplied to a non-resident who is outside New Zealand at the time the services are performed (section 11A), except services directly connected with real property in New Zealand or certain personal services physically performed in New Zealand. A portable solar power retail business qualifies for zero-ratings on outbound goods exports, but online digital services (e.g., downloads) supplied to non-residents may also be zero-rated where the recipient's normal place of residence is outside New Zealand.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration (CusDec) submitted through the New Zealand Trade Single Window (or a copy of the Bill of Entry for the export shipment)
Bill of Lading (sea freight) or Airway Bill (air freight) evidencing that the goods left New Zealand
Commercial invoice and packing list describing the goods and their destination

Inward Remittance Certificate (IRC) or bank/Stripe payment records clearly showing that the consideration was received from an offshore account in the name of the non-resident purchaser (or a certificate issued by the receiving New Zealand bank confirming the overseas origin of funds)
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 and the Tax Administration Act 1994, if zero-rating is applied without sufficient supporting evidence, the supplier is liable for the unpaid GST at 15% plus interest. The Inland Revenue may impose a shortfall penalty of 20% for lack of reasonable care, 40% for gross carelessness, 100% for an abusive tax position, and 150% for evasion or fraudulent intent. If documents are found false or fraudulent, the IRD can disallow the zero-rating retrospectively and assess GST on the original supply date, with backdated interest and penalties. willful evasion may also lead to criminal prosecution, fines of up to NZD 50,000 for individuals (and up to NZD 250,000 for companies), and potential imprisonment. In practice, the IRD scrutinises export records for consistency between the customs declaration, transport documents, and the foreign exchange receipts; any unexplained gap beyond the 28-day export rule triggers a reassessment and clawback.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Te Putea Matua) acting also as the prudential regulator and financial stability authority; exchange control functions reside with the Reserve Bank of New Zealand under the Banking Act and the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013, with no separate foreign exchange administration.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: New Zealand operates a widely recognized free-floating exchange rate regime with full convertibility of the New Zealand dollar (NZD) on both the current account and capital account. There are no statutory exchange control restrictions, no prior government approval requirements for cross-border transfers, and no limits on the repatriation of profits, dividends, or invested capital for foreign-owned entities. The Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 and the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 impose compliance obligations but do not restrict currency movement. Companies can maintain foreign currency bank accounts, invoice in multiple currencies, and convert NZD to any foreign currency at market rates without surrender obligations. Profit remittance hurdles are minimal and generally only require standard corporate governance approvals (board resolution) and tax clearance from Inland Revenue to demonstrate that withholding tax obligations have been settled. A commercial bank may request supporting transactional documentation to satisfy its own internal cross-border payment acceptance policy. The absence of surrender requirements and capital controls makes New Zealand a highly efficient jurisdiction for a cross-border e-commerce treasury operation, provided the entity maintains robust AML/KYC files for all counterparties and complies with tax reporting under the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA) and the Common Reporting Standard (CRS) where applicable.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: No statutory requirement. Export proceeds in foreign currency are not required to be surrendered to the Reserve Bank of New Zealand or any domestic bank. The exporter may retain foreign currency indefinitely, convert to NZD at any time, or use funds directly to satisfy overseas operational liabilities. The default conversion ratio is 0% mandatory; however, if a receivable is settled in a foreign currency, the company may voluntarily choose to convert any portion into NZD subject to the bank's normal foreign exchange pricing and transaction due diligence. The only documentary requirement is accurate record-keeping for tax and financial reporting under the Financial Reporting Act 2013.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Limited (New Zealand) (ANZ)
tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Business Transaction Account (NZD) with Foreign Currency Basket and Capital Escrow Capability
ASB Business Current Account plus Offshore Foreign Currency Account (multi-currency)
BNZ Business Plus Account with Multi-Currency Facility and Online Settlement
Westpac Business Cash Management Account with Revolving FX and Global Trade Services

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: High with legal structuring. Offshore digital EMI platforms (e.g. Stripe, Airwallex, Wise Business) may legally service a New Zealand-registered entity, but they must comply with the Financial Service Providers (Registration and Dispute Resolution) Act 2008 (FSP Act). To hold customer funds and execute NZD domestically, an EMI must either be registered as a New Zealand financial service provider or operate through a licensed New Zealand commercial bank partner. Stripe uses a third-party NZ bank sponsorship for local NZD collection and payout; Airwallex holds an authorised deposit-taking institution (ADI) status in Australia, which allows them to offer NZD payment services through cross-border partnerships. A pure fintech EMI without FSP registration and AML/CFT compliance cannot legally service New Zealand entities. The viability for a low-risk e-commerce retailer is high when using established EMIs that partner with major NZ banks, but the primary operating account should remain with a Tier-1 domestic bank to ensure reliable clearing, capital verification, and future credit access. The treasury design should use the EMI for customer payment intake (Stripe, Affirm) and the Tier-1 bank as the ultimate settlement hub.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: There is no statutory requirement for directors to appear physically in-branch in New Zealand. The anti-money laundering framework under the AML/CFT Act accepts a risk-based approach to customer verification, allowing banks to conduct remote electronic identity verification via digital ID (e.g. NZ Post's RealMe.govt.nz, or FaceTec via the bank's app). However, the first corporate account application for a non-resident-owned limited company typically requires: (1) certified copy of the Certificate of Incorporation from the New Zealand Companies Office; (2) certified passports and proof of address for both directors and ultimate beneficial owners; (3) notarised or apostilled copies of the trust deed or corporate registry extract if the shareholder is a legal arrangement; (4) for wholly online onboarding, a video interview may be accepted if the compliance committee assesses the jurisdiction and customer risk as low. In practice, Westpac, ASB, and BNZ accept remote video KYC for online retail entities, while ANZ may require a physical visit to a branch for non-prime jurisdictions. Since the entity is a standard low-risk online retailer, remote onboarding is highly feasible with a recognised digital ID provider, but the bank may still request a physically present New Zealand-resident director or a local professional (e.g. accountant or lawyer) to verify the document copies. We strongly recommend appointing a local company secretary or using a New Zealand registered office service to expedite onboarding.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Source of initial capital injection into the New Zealand entity from offshore shareholders (non-resident natural persons) triggers enhanced due diligence under New Zealand AML/CFT Section 22, especially when the payer is a domestic trust or a private bank in a high-risk jurisdiction.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide a comprehensive capital funding file: (1) original signed board resolution from the foreign shareholder approving the capital injection; (2) six months of bank statements from the remitting bank showing the source of wealth/accumulated earnings; (3) audited financial statements of the shareholder entity or tax return/beneficiary statement if the shareholder is a trust; (4) notarised and apostilled copies of the trust deed or corporate certificate; (5) beneficial ownership declaration (IRL 753 form) listing all individuals owning 25% or more; (6) a sworn declaration of lawful source of funds, endorsed by a certified accountant registered in the payee jurisdiction.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Verification of ultimate beneficial ownership (UBO) is challenging when the NZ_LTD is owned by another offshore vehicle in a tax-haven jurisdiction, which is automatically categorised as high-risk, leading to refusal of remote onboarding.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Prepare a UBO disclosure pack: (1) a transparent corporate ownership diagram linking NZ_LTD to each ultimate natural person; (2) official company registry extract of each intermediate entity (with updated register of members); (3) notarised passport copies of all UBOs; (4) independent credit agency background check (e.g. World-Check or Dow Jones) proving no sanctions or adverse media; (5) a written explanation of the commercial rationale for the offshore holding structure, referencing the solar retail business model and APAC intellectual property licensing; (6) legal opinion from a qualified New Zealand solicitor confirming that the structure is not a shell or sham entity.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High volume of cross-border e-commerce customer payments from multiple jurisdictions via Stripe and Affirm BNPL triggers a bank's suspicion that the entity is operating as an unregulated payment facilitator or mixing personal funds with business revenue.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide transactional evidence: (1) Stripe and Affirm gateway settlement reports with payment source country mapping and daily volume/pricing; (2) refund and dispute logs to demonstrate genuine retail activity; (3) e-commerce sales invoices with unique order IDs and IP geolocation of customers; (4) merchandise shipping proof (tracking numbers and courier receipts) to substantiate actual goods movement; (5) a compliance manual showing customer due diligence, sanctions screening, and fraud control procedures at the payment processor level; (6) an independent accounting firm's Interim Review Report (NZSA Review Engagement) of sales revenue and cash flow.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Remittance of profits or management fees to the overseas parent during the first year of operation activates additional scrutiny because the bank cannot confirm the operating substance or the true commercial benefit for the NZ entity.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Assemble an economic substance file: (1) audited financial statements for the first six months demonstrating genuine operating expenditure (inventory purchases, logistics, IT); (2) payroll records of New Zealand-based staff or contractor agreements (or an outsourced service agreement with a local e-commerce fulfilment centre); (3) a detailed transfer pricing policy under NZ Income Tax Act 2007 s GC15-17 showing arm's length management fees; (4) board meeting minutes approving the outbound remittance with a formal profit distribution or service fee valuation; (5) a tax clearance certificate issued by Inland Revenue confirming PAYE, GST, and any withholding tax are settled; (6) bank's own questionnaire confirming that the remittance will not generate a tax loss for NZ_LTD.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound capital injections into NZ_LTD should be routed via SWIFT MT103 with clear reference field 70 offering the purpose of payment code P-ACCESS1 (IFS Direct Investment) or using the New Zealand standard tax category for inbound services. Since New Zealand has no exchange controls, the funds can be remitted in NZD or USD and converted by the receiving bank at floating market rate. The receiving Tier-1 bank may require a completed International Transaction Reporting System (ITRS) form for balance-of-payments statistics. Capital verification is performed by the company's external auditor using the bank's stamped confirmation, the MT103 inbound telegram, and the shareholder resolution. Recommend using a dedicated inbound capital escrow account at the primary Tier-1 bank (e.g. ANZ 'Capital Escrow Account') where funds are held until the Companies Office registry is updated with share allotments. The purpose code should be 'A56010 – Direct Investment – Equity Capital' to avoid delays. Any subsequent parent loans should be reported as 'Investment Loan – Equity Structure' and will require a written loan agreement with arm's length interest rate to avoid attribution to Inland Revenue.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: For trade settlements, use SWIFT MT103 for routine supplier payments under USD 50,000, with reference field 70 reflecting the commercial invoice number and ISIC 4791 e-commerce order reference. For large inventory purchases (e.g. bulk solar panel procurement from Asia), use an irrevocable and confirmed Commercial Letter of Credit (L/C) with a sight tenor or a 90-day usance, added in the remittance instruction. Documentary Collections (D/P and D/A) are permissible for high-trust suppliers, but not recommended for first-time transactions. All outbound FX payments must be submitted with a Statement of Account and the relevant trade document (invoice and packing list) to satisfy the bank's cross-border payment control desk. For everyday operational costs (logistics, warehousing, and payment processor fees), use the bank's online corporate banking gateway with Multi-Currency Account (e.g. BNZ's 'GlobalPlus' or Westpac's 'FX Online') to transact in USD, CNY, and AUD with automatic settlement. Payment processor payouts from Stripe (in NZD) should be concentrated into the base account on a daily T+1 basis, and Affirm BNPL should be reconciled monthly via its merchant payout CSV. The treasury policy must maintain a segregated client/operational funds separate from the merchant settlement account. SWIFT MT103 payments to mainland China must be routed via a correspondent bank under the 'China Foreign Exchange Payment System' (CIPS) format and include the Chinese payment code (e.g. 121010) in field 70.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable FX forward contracts with settlement in New Zealand dollars, tenor up to 12 months, available from all four major banks for commercial exposures; requires underlying trade invoice or purchase order.

FX options (European style, plain vanilla) on NZD/USD and NZD/CNY with a tenor up to 6 months, sold by domestic banks for hedge accounting alignment; options are permissible for genuine exposure hedging and are not prohibited for the online retail sector.

Cross-currency interest rate swaps (CIRS) between NZD and USD for converting floating rate borrowings into a different currency, permitted if the entity has a current asset-liability mismatch; stringent documentation under the Swap Agreement and a board resolution are required.

Non-deliverable forward (NDF) contracts are permissible for offshore counterparties when the underlying remittance is in a non-convertible or restricted currency (e.g. certain emerging market currencies) but are not commonly used for NZD itself because the NZD is fully deliverable; any NDF must be transacted through an approved international bank with clearing house designation and reported to the Reserve Bank of New Zealand for statistical monitoring.

Currency swaps via a foreign exchange swap (FX Swap) transaction with spot and forward legs, restricted to actual cash flow forecasting and same-day liquidity management, with no speculative positions allowed under the bank's credit policy.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Return under the Companies Act 1993 (Section 242) - NZD 10 online / NZD 30 paper
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Registrar of Companies, New Zealand Companies Office (Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: By the company's annual return date recorded on the New Zealand Companies Register, normally the anniversary of incorporation; early filing is permitted up to three months before the annual return date.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: If the Annual Return remains unfiled, the Registrar may issue a notice requiring rectification; after not less than 20 working days notice the company is liable to administrative strike-off and dissolution under Part 18 of the Companies Act 1993, with potential director disqualification and personal liability for trading while struck off.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Company Income Tax Return (IR4) with income tax reconciliation and, where required, tax support accounts and financial statements
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Inland Revenue Department (IRD) - Te Tari Taake
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: For a standard 31 March balance date, filing is due by 7 July following balance date; for a non-standard balance date, by the 7th day of the 7th month after balance date. Terminal income tax for a 31 March balance date is due by 7 April, or as prescribed for non-standard balance dates.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing incurs an initial penalty of NZD 250 and a further NZD 500 if the return is still outstanding after 180 days; late payment penalties begin at 1% of the unpaid tax and accrue at 1.5% per month, plus statutory use-of-money interest at IRD prescribed rates.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Goods and Services Tax (GST) Return for each monthly, two-monthly, or six-monthly taxable period
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Inland Revenue Department (IRD) - Te Tari Taake
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due by the 28th day after the end of each GST taxable period, or the 30th day for myIR online filers; where the company has approved a non-standard taxable period, the same quarterly and monthly filing-cycle rules apply.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing penalty is NZD 250, with an additional NZD 500 after 180 days; late payment penalties start at 1% and continue at 1.5% per month, plus statutory use-of-money interest at IRD applicable rates.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Fringe Benefit Tax Annual Return (IR429) - applicable only where the employer provides fringe benefits and has elected annual filing
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Inland Revenue Department (IRD) - Te Tari Taake
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: By 7 July following the 31 March tax year, or by the 7th day of the 7th month after the company's approved non-standard balance date.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing penalty of NZD 250 and an additional NZD 500 after 180 days; late payment penalties and use-of-money interest accrue at IRD statutory rates until fully settled.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Audited Financial Statements and statutory financial report delivery (where the company is large, overseas-owned, or otherwise required under the Financial Reporting Act 2013)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Shareholders at the annual shareholder meeting and, where filing is required, the Registrar of Companies, New Zealand Companies Office (MBIE)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Financial statements must be prepared and, if statutorily required, audited within 5 months of balance date; where filing with the Registrar is required, the audited financial statements must also be filed within that 5-month statutory window.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Directors may receive infringement notices, the company may be referred for enforcement action, and persistent non-compliance may expose directors to pecuniary penalties, infringement fees, and company removal proceedings.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual internal statutory register audit and board confirmation of share register, director register, charges register, and minute book
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Company board of directors and registered office agent in New Zealand
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: At least once per financial year, ordinarily completed before the Annual Return filing date and ratified by board resolution.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: There is no direct government filing fee for the internal self-audit, but inaccurate registers may constitute a director duty breach, produce incorrect shareholder or charge priority records, and expose the company to infringement fees and third-party claims.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: In New Zealand, an independent statutory audit is compulsory for an ordinary Limited company that is a large company under the Financial Reporting Act 2013, meaning total assets equal or exceed NZD 60 million at balance date, annual revenue equal or exceeds NZD 30 million, or the company has 50 or more full-time-equivalent employees during the accounting period. An audit is also mandatory where the company is an FMC reporting entity under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013, is in a group containing a large company or FMC reporting entity, or is an overseas-owned company required to file financial statements. A shareholder or shareholders holding at least 5% of the voting shares may requisition an independent audit under Section 199 of the Companies Act 1993, and the company constitution may also impose a stricter audit requirement. Companies falling below the large thresholds and not otherwise requiring audit are exempt from mandatory audit, provided they are not FMC reporting entities, are not overseas-owned, and are not part of a large group.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Financial statements must be prepared in accordance with XRB-approved accounting standards: NZ IFRS for Tier 1 and public-accountability reporting entities, NZ IFRS Reduced Disclosure Regime or NZ IFRS for SMEs for smaller

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No general federal tax holidays; certain R&D tax credits (15% on eligible R&D expenditure) available under the Research and Development Tax Incentive; no patent box regime; free-zone incentives not applicable in New Zealand.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: IRC 103 / IR4 – Income Tax Return for Companies; filed electronically via myIR (Inland Revenue Department's online portal). For non-resident companies with NZ source income, use IR4NZ (Non-Resident Company Income Tax Return) where applicable.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Due no later than the 7th day of the month following the company's balance-date anniversary filing day as notified by Inland Revenue; most balance-date companies file by 31 March tax year, with terminal tax due 7 April following year-end. If a tax agent is engaged, extended due dates apply under section 44 of the Tax Administration Act 1994.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Declare gross income derived from all sources, including New Zealand-source online retail sales of solar portable power products. For e-commerce sales, source is determined under section OE 4 of the Income Tax Act 2007: income from sales is generally sourced where the vendor's business is carried on; ensure online platform sales to New Zealand consumers are fully reported.

Declare any non-trading income such as interest, royalties, or foreign exchange gains. Non-resident companies must isolate New Zealand-sourced interest and royalty income, as it may be subject to gross basis non-resident withholding tax rather than standard corporate tax rates.

Record income adjustments including deemed interest under transfer pricing recharacterisation, thin-capitalisation interest adjustments (section GG 1 – GG 15), and accrual adjustments. If an NZ subsidiary sells inventory cross-border to an offshore affiliate, apply the arm's length principle under Part F of the Income Tax Act 2007.

Claim deductions only for expenses incurred in deriving assessable income. Non-resident companies must not deduct head-office overhead recharged without full transfer pricing documentation; also reverse any non-deductible interest expense disallowed under thin capitalisation where debt exceeds 60% of total assets.

Calculate net income after allowable deductions. Losses of a non-resident company are ring-fenced if the company is not carrying on business in New Zealand through a fixed establishment; otherwise, losses may be available for carry-forward subject to the shareholder continuity rules (sections IA 5 – IA 9).

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tax credits and non-resident withholding tax credits (excluding PAYE)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Claim credits for NZ resident withholding tax (RWT) deducted from interest and dividends, foreign dividend withholding payments, and imputation credits attached to dividends received from NZ resident companies. Ensure that any dividends repatriated offshore are declared in this box for the shareholder dividend statement.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty: NZ$250 for each month or part month the return is late, capped (for most companies) at NZ$5,000. Late payment penalty imposes an initial 1% of unpaid tax, followed by a 4% incremental penalty applied monthly. Use-of-money interest (currently 8.9% for underpayment) accrues on any unpaid terminal tax from the due date until paid. Knowingly filing a false return constitutes tax evasion under section 143B of the Tax Administration Act 1994, carrying a maximum fine of NZ$50,000 and/or up to 5 years' imprisonment; evasion of a large amount (over NZ$100,000) may attract up to 7 years' imprisonment.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 30% (final withholding tax on dividends paid to non-residents, subject to reduction under a Double Tax Agreement).
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To claim reduced NZ withholding tax under an applicable DTA, the non-resident shareholder must deliver to the NZ payer (via the IR719 Non-Resident Certificate or IR67F withholding payment form) a completed declaration of tax residence in the treaty jurisdiction together with a valid Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) issued by the foreign tax authority. The certificate must demonstrate the recipient is the beneficial owner of the dividend and is entitled to treaty benefits under the limitation-of-benefits / predominant-intent test in the applicable DTA. For Australia, schedular withholding rates of 0–15% may apply under the NZ–Australia DTA; for most other treaty partners, the dividend rate is 15% (5% if the beneficial owner is a company holding at least 10% voting share capital), provided the required IR67F form is filed with Inland Revenue before the payment is made.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory rates: 15% on interest and 15% on royalties (under the Non-Resident Withholding Tax regime, although the approved issuer levy (AIL) of 2% can apply to interest if the lender is an offshore associated party not subject to RWT). Treaty rates typically reduce interest and royalty withholding to 10% under most NZ DTAs, subject to the recipient being beneficial owner and providing an IR67F declaration with a TRC. Interest paid to an Australian resident may be exempt under NZ domestic law if the AIL is paid, and royalties to Australian residents may be subject to 5% treaty rate if the rights are used in Australia.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: New Zealand applies transfer pricing documentation rules (sections GC 6 – GC 13 of the Income Tax Act 2007) but does not prescribe a specific local currency threshold for mandatory contemporaneous documentation. Inland Revenue's Operational Statement 17/02 requires entities with cross-border related-party transactions to prepare and maintain Transfer Pricing Documentation (Local File, Master File, and Country-by-Country Report if the group consolidates above NZ$1.3 billion) on a self-assessment basis; practical thresholds approximate NZ$1 million for intercompany services/loans and NZ$3 million for goods transactions, below which simplified documentation may be acceptable.
approved_arm_length_methodologies: CUP, Resale Price, Cost Plus, TNMM, Profit Split
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: New Zealand applies the Economic Substance Requirement through the general anti-avoidance rule (sections BG 1 and GA 1) and specific transfer pricing rules. A non-resident company or a New Zealand company in a multinational group must demonstrate real commercial activity, with strategic decision-making, key assets, and core income-generating activities (CIGA) located in New Zealand for income attribution. The absence of substance triggers a reallocation of profits by the Commissioner under section GC 1(1); shell companies with no local employees or premises risk having their intercompany payments disallowed and profits reconstructed. Relevant CIGA for online retail includes procurement, inventory ownership, pricing algorithms, fulfilment (unless contracted), and customer support.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Knowingly underreporting or omitting online sales revenue derived from New Zealand customers, using offshore shell payment entities, or fabricating deductions to reduce taxable income below the true amount.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Sections 143A and 143B of the Tax Administration Act 1994: fine up to NZ$50,000 plus unpaid tax; section 143C evasion of assessment imposes additional penalties of up to 200% of the tax evaded; imprisonment up to 5 years (7 years for amounts exceeding NZ$100,000).
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly assist in tax evasion breach the Companies Act 1993 section 135 duties and the Financial Reporting Act; the corporate veil is pierced under section 193 of the Companies Act 1993 for dishonest or fraudulent conduct. Directors face civil liability for the company's unpaid tax only if they have knowingly participated in the evasion and personally benefited; travel bans may be imposed under section 171 of the Tax Administration Act 1994 (taxpayer blacklisting / departure prohibition orders) for unpaid assessments exceeding NZ$20,000, and criminal conviction carries imprisonment.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Mis-pricing cross-border purchases of portable solar panels from a related Hong Kong or Singapore supplier, or charging inflated management fees and intellectual property royalties to erode the New Zealand taxable base without arm's length comparables.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Income Tax Act 2007 section GC 1 – the Commissioner may reconstruct the transaction to reflect the arm's length amount; section GB 2(1B) applies a non-deductibility adjustment and assesses additional tax; late payment penalties and use-of-money interest apply under the Tax Administration Act 1994; shortfall penalties under section 141B range from 20% (not taking reasonable care) to 150% (abusive tax position) of the resulting tax shortfall.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who sign or cause the company to file false transfer pricing documentation commit an offence under section 143H of the Tax Administration Act, punishable by a fine up to NZ$50,000 and imprisonment up to 3 years for wilful obstruction or knowing false statement; the Court may order the director to repay personal benefits received from the profit shifting and may freeze assets. Inland Revenue may issue a departure prohibition order preventing directors from leaving New Zealand while substantial tax liabilities remain outstanding.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: The New Zealand company is established as a mere conduit with no warehouse, employees, or actual logistics; online sales contracts are booked by a related Hong Kong entity while the NZ Ltd exists solely to provide a 'New Zealand origin' label and access to free-trade agreement certificates of origin for solar products.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: General anti-avoidance rule (section BG 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007) invalidates the tax advantage; the Commissioner may disregard the structure and treat the underlying economic substance as being in New Zealand (section GB 1); failure to file accurate CbC reports or master file under the OECD BEPS standards incurs civil penalties up to NZ$20,000 under sections 78EBC and 78EBR of the Tax Administration Act 1994; providing false import/export documentation violates the Customs and Excise Act 2018 (offence under section 369) with penalties of up to NZ$50,000 plus triple the unpaid duty.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors are personally liable as shadow directors under section 8 of the Companies Act 1993 if the shell arrangement amounts to insolvent trading or fraud. Under the veil-piercing test in section 193, if the company is used for a dishonest purpose, directors can be ordered to pay restitution for all avoided taxes plus interest. The same conduct may constitute a criminal offence of obtaining pecuniary advantage by dishonesty under section 228 of the Crimes Act 1961, punishable by imprisonment of up to 7 years. Directors may also be banned from managing a company for up to 5 years under section 383 of the Companies Act 1993.
